data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) has kept inflation low under a managed float: 3.5% in 2008 on the commodity boom, then 0-2% through the 2010s (with mild deflation in 2009, 2015, and 2020), rising to 2.9% in 2022 and easing to a projected 1.7% in 2025. The central bank is famously conservative, hiking less than peers in 2022 and relying on the currency and administered prices. Expectations are firmly anchored; Taiwan never experienced the post-COVID inflation surge seen elsewhere.
debt_management: Taiwan's public debt has declined steadily, from 33.3% of GDP in 2006 to a projected 22.4% in 2025, one of Asia's best trajectories. Strong growth (GDP from $386.4bn to a projected $920.0bn), fiscal surpluses in good years, and conservative budgeting explain the improvement; even COVID only nudged the ratio from 32.6% (2019) to 32.0% (2020). The government has fiscal space it rarely uses. Contingent needs are defense spending, which is rising with cross-strait tensions, and energy transition costs.

key_events.event: Global crisis; exports collapsed then rebounded on Chinese stimulus demand.
Sunflower Movement protests blocked a services trade pact with China.
Tsai Ing-wen and the DPP won, shifting cross-strait policy.
COVID-19 contained with minimal lockdowns; tech exports boomed.
Global chip shortage made TSMC central to geopolitics; drought tested resilience.
Pelosi's August visit triggered Chinese military exercises and tensions.
Lai Ching-te elected president; cross-strait tensions remained elevated.

outlook_next_decade: Taiwan's base case is 2-3% growth on semiconductor dominance (TSMC's expansion abroad included), with low inflation and falling debt. The dominant risk is geopolitical: cross-strait tensions could disrupt trade and investment, though economic interdependence cuts both ways. Energy security (nuclear phase-out debates) and demographic aging are secondary drags. Analytical assessment: macro fundamentals are excellent; the risk premium is almost entirely geopolitical.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
